subsystems.name: Detection and tracking network
subsystems.role: find incoming interstellar objects early enough to plan an intercept.

subsystems.name: Interceptor spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: a pre-positioned platform that can loiter for years then execute a high-speed flyby.
parts: power system (solar arrays or radioisotope generator)

subsystems.name: Propulsion system
subsystems.role: provide the large velocity change needed to reach an object moving fast relative to the Sun.

subsystems.name: Science instrument suite
subsystems.role: measure composition, structure and dust environment at encounter.

subsystems.name: Communications and navigation
subsystems.role: return data and steer the spacecraft autonomously at high closing speed.

subsystems.name: Encounter sub-probes
subsystems.role: increase chances of a close look by releasing small probes before flyby.

buildSteps.title: Choose a waiting strategy
buildSteps.detail: Decide where to park the interceptor — for example, a stable orbit at the Sun–Earth L2 point or a heliocentric orbit — so it can reach a range of incoming objects with limited fuel.

buildSteps.title: Design the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: Trade propulsion type against target reach; a high-speed flyby needs tens of kilometres per second of velocity change, which may require chemical stages plus gravity assists.

buildSteps.title: Build and test the bus
buildSteps.detail: Assemble the structure, avionics, power and thermal systems, then test in thermal-vacuum and vibration facilities to survive launch and deep space.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the instruments
buildSteps.detail: Mount cameras, spectrometers and dust detectors, and calibrate them before launch.

buildSteps.title: Launch and park
buildSteps.detail: Launch on a rocket to the waiting orbit; the spacecraft enters a low-activity mode, keeping systems alive for years.

buildSteps.title: Detect a target
buildSteps.detail: Ground survey telescopes discover a new interstellar object and quickly determine its orbit; an alert triggers the interceptor.

buildSteps.title: Compute and execute the intercept
buildSteps.detail: Within days, calculate a trajectory that intercepts the object, then fire engines or begin ion-thrusting, possibly using a planetary flyby for extra speed.

buildSteps.title: Flyby and return data
buildSteps.detail: At encounter, instruments take rapid measurements and the spacecraft transmits them back to Earth over weeks or months.

prerequisites.why: they exist, but an interstellar object is usually found only weeks before it is closest to the Sun, leaving little time to react.
ion engines give high efficiency but low thrust; chemical rockets give thrust but need large tanks to reach the tens of km/s required.

prerequisites.tech: Autonomous navigation and rapid trajectory design
prerequisites.why: a spacecraft must target a fast-moving object with little ground intervention, and the orbit must be computed within days.
solar arrays work near the Sun; radioisotope generators power missions far out, as used by past outer-planet probes.
deep-space antennas can receive data, but the encounter is brief and data rates are low.

pathway.milestone: survey telescopes discover interstellar objects (1I/Oumuamua in 2017, 2I/Borisov in 2019) but no spacecraft can reach them.
pathway.unlocks: catalogs of orbits and growing evidence that such objects are common.

pathway.milestone: a European mission (Comet Interceptor) plans to wait at L2 for a comet, with the possibility of an interstellar object, but it will not intercept a specific known object.
pathway.unlocks: experience in parking and rapid targeting.

pathway.milestone: dedicated interceptor studies (such as Project Lyra) model high-speed flybys using Jupiter gravity assists.
pathway.unlocks: concrete mission designs and propulsion requirements.

pathway.milestone: pre-positioned interceptors ready for launch on short notice, perhaps using solar sails or nuclear thermal propulsion.
pathway.unlocks: direct composition measurements of material from other planetary systems.
